newsitem.title: UK: Russia, U.S. provide impetus for emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: Russia, U.S. provide impetus for emerging markets.

text.p: Developments in Russia and key U.S. figures will provide the impetus for investors across emerging markets this week, analysts said.
Rumours that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had died rippled through stock and debt markets last week and strategists see more volatility in the weeks ahead.
"Yeltsin's health is an issue that's going to drag on," said ING Barings global strategist Matthew Merritt.

"The market is beginning to buy the view that the planks for economic reform are in place and that Russia has moved a long way -- hence the ratings last week," he said. "The larger investor will be looking for any volatility to start picking up stocks."

He said the economic background for investors -- dollar strength, mark weakness and the convergence of debt yield spreads throughout Europe -- was an attractive backdrop not just for Russia but for emerging Europe as a whole.
Russia itself is due to launch its debut Eurobond within the next three weeks following the assignment of high speculative grade ratings.
Yeltsin is due to meet Belarussian leader Alexander Lukashenko in Moscow, and investors hope this will dispel nerves over his well-being ahead of his heart bypass operation.

Fixed income investors will continue to monitor Bulgaria for news on whether the International Monetary Fund will provide the delayed second tranche of a standby loan. Access to the cash depends on Sofia's ability to convince the Fund it is moving ahead with economic reforms.

Meanwhile US data due during the week will continue to set the emerging market scene. Friday's U.S. retail sales data came in higher than expected but the August figure was revised down and analysts said the outlook for inflation was still benign.
A weaker number would have helped fixed income investors, especially those in Latin American debt. Capital flows out of Asia have already boosted Bradys.
Brazil is expected to launch a global bond, possibly as high as $1.0 billion, during the week, with punters tipping Wednesday as the most likely day.

On the political front, a congressional committee will begin discussions in the next two weeks on whether to amend the constitution to allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for re-election.

The government had been expected to set up the committee this week but the move was delayed to give the Brazilian Progresive Party -- one of the four biggest -- time to decide its position on the re-election question.
Brazil is due to announce September trade figures this week. ING Barings is looking for a number close to $4.2 billion, which will produce a trade deficit between $300 and $400 million.

The president of Chile, Eduardo Frei, begins an official visit to the United Kingdom today when he addresses the Confederation of British Industry. Chile has municipal elections on October 27, seen as a crucial test of Frei's standing.

Equity investors in Asia will be keeping an anxious eye on the stock market in Thailand, which plumbed three-year lows last week. Blue chip stocks, especially banks are expected to take a further battering.

Some technical analysts say Singapore is likely to come under pressure in the short term, with big falls possible. "The big question mark in Asia as a region is when do you move back in on mass," Merritt said. "The fear that is keeping people away is the possibility of a correction in U.S. Treasuries."
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was off 0.9 percent at 298.79 points on Friday from a week previously.
Latin America was at 548.12, up 0.2 percent while Asia was 2.2 percent lower at 249.06. Europe, Middle East and Africa was quoted at 142.55, off one percentage point on the previous week.
